title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's October 12, 2008 Inquirer column on the Judicial and Bar Council's responsibility to nominate worthy justices for the seven Supreme Court vacancies of 2009, an unprecedented turnover of nearly half the Court in a single year

Why the responsibility falls 'squarely on the JBC': since the President may appoint only from the JBC's list of at least three per vacancy, 'even if just one undeserving candidate is smuggled into the list, the whole selection process tumbles' -- so the three 's' functions (search, screen, select) 'cannot afford a single mistake'

The hard part -- finding the four nonquantifiable qualities ('proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' especially independence and integrity) beyond the three quantifiable ones (natural-born, at least 40, 15 years' practice)

Praiseworthy monitoring and transparency initiatives -- Pangilinan's 'Bantay Korte Suprema,' Dimayuga's California-style reference checks, and Castro's proposal to record and publish JBC votes -- which CJP endorses by analogy to the public votes of justices
sub_topics: The unprecedented turnover: the JBC must fill seven Supreme Court vacancies created by seven retirements in 2009 -- 'never in the normal history of the Court has almost one-half of its membership changed within just one year' (excluding the 1986 Aquino revolutionary 'judicial cleansing')

Where responsibility lies: because the President's choice is 'restricted only to those nominated by the council' and judicial appointments are no longer passed on by the Commission on Appointments, 'the primary responsibility for choosing worthy justices falls squarely on the JBC'

The single-mistake stakes: if the JBC nominates only the most qualified, every appointment is 'unquestionable,' but 'even if just one undeserving candidate is smuggled into the list, the whole selection process tumbles' -- so the three 's' functions (search, screen, select) admit no error

The qualifications: the Constitution's three quantifiable requirements (natural-born citizen, at least 40, at least 15 years of law practice or lower-court judgeship) and four nonquantifiable qualities ('proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence'), of which independence and integrity are 'the most elusive but most essential'

The first vacancy and a procedural gripe: the process for the seat opening when Justice Ruben T. Reyes retires on January 2, 2009 had begun, but the JBC's October 13 application deadline was 'not generally known' and, CJP urges, 'should be extended'

Monitoring the JBC: he praises Senator Kiko Pangilinan's 'Bantay Korte Suprema' (inviting the legal community, academe, civil society and business to participate) and Dean Amado Dimayuga's reference-check system -- modeled on California's Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission -- in which applicants list courts and legal references, survey forms go to randomly picked references, and the JBC evaluates from at least 20 responses

Judging the JBC: he backs J. Conrado Castro's proposal to record and make public the JBC members' votes (now by secret ballot), so that 'when magistrates misbehave,' responsibility for their appointment can be pinpointed -- reasoning that since 'the votes of individual justices in all Supreme Court decisions... are made known,' JBC votes should not be hidden, because 'transparency... breeds public confidence'

The charge to the Council: the JBC must nominate 'only... the most eminent, not... who barely qualify,' and 'will be praised or condemned by the quality of all their choices' -- its members listed as CJ Puno (chair), Justice Secretary Raul Gonzalez, Rep. Matias Defensor Jr., retired Justices Regino Hermosisima Jr. and Aurora Lagman, plus Pangilinan, Dimayuga and Castro

stances.claim: With the President confined to the JBC's list and no Commission-on-Appointments backstop, 'the primary responsibility for choosing worthy justices falls squarely on the JBC' -- and because 'one undeserving candidate' can taint everything, its search-screen-select work 'cannot afford a single mistake,' especially in filling seven seats at once in 2009.
stances.rhetorical_move: stakes-amplification: tying the gravity of an unprecedented turnover to the JBC's zero-error duty

stances.claim: The hardest task is finding the 'nonquantifiable' qualities -- above all independence and integrity -- beyond the easy quantifiable ones, which is the JBC's 'ultimate task.'
stances.rhetorical_move: difficulty-naming: distinguishing checkbox credentials from the elusive virtues that actually matter

stances.claim: Transparency and monitoring should be embraced -- Pangilinan's Bantay Korte Suprema, Dimayuga's reference checks, and especially Castro's proposal to make JBC votes public -- because, just as 'the votes of individual justices... are made known,' open JBC voting would 'pinpoint responsibility' and 'breed public confidence.'
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy-driven endorsement: justifying public JBC votes by parallel to the already-public votes of justices

notable_anecdotes: Half the Court in one year: CJP underscores that the seven 2009 vacancies mean 'almost one-half' of the Court would change in a single year -- unprecedented outside the 1986 revolutionary cleansing.
The hidden deadline: he flags that the JBC's October 13 application deadline for the first vacancy (Justice Reyes's seat) was 'not generally known' and should be extended.

The California model: he describes Dean Dimayuga's reference-check system -- borrowed from California's Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission -- in which survey forms go to at least 20 randomly chosen references before the JBC evaluates a candidate.
'Will they pass the test?': he closes by warning that the JBC 'will be praised or condemned by the quality of all their choices,' naming its members so readers know who is accountable.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's October 12, 2008 Inquirer column, examines the Judicial and Bar Council's responsibility to nominate worthy justices for the seven Supreme Court vacancies of 2009 -- an unprecedented turnover of 'almost one-half' the Court in a single year (outside the 1986 Aquino revolutionary 'cleansing'). Because the President may appoint only from the JBC's list of at least three per vacancy and judicial appointments no longer pass through the Commission on Appointments, 'the primary responsibility... falls squarely on the JBC': if it nominates only the most qualified, every appointment is 'unquestionable,' but 'even if just one undeserving candidate is smuggled into the list, the whole selection process tumbles' -- so its three 's' functions (search, screen, select) 'cannot afford a single mistake.' The hard part, he says, is finding the four nonquantifiable qualities ('proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' especially the last two) beyond the three quantifiable ones (natural-born, at least 40, 15 years' practice). He notes the process for the first vacancy (Justice Ruben Reyes's seat, opening January 2, 2009) had begun but the October 13 application deadline was 'not generally known' and should be extended. He praises three monitoring and transparency efforts: Senator Pangilinan's 'Bantay Korte Suprema,' which invites the legal community, academe, civil society and business to take part; Dean Dimayuga's reference-check system, modeled on California's Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission, which surveys at least 20 references before the JBC evaluates a candidate; and J. Conrado Castro's proposal to record and publish the JBC's votes, now cast by secret ballot. Reasoning that since 'the votes of individual justices... are made known,' open JBC voting would 'pinpoint responsibility' when 'magistrates misbehave' and 'breed public confidence,' he endorses it. The JBC, he concludes, must nominate 'only... the most eminent' and 'will be praised or condemned by the quality of all their choices' -- naming the members so readers know who is accountable: 'Will they pass the test?'
